promptText: A write-heavy service is struggling to keep up with insert volume, and the team's proposed fix is "add more read replicas." Why does this fail to address the actual problem?
options: Replicas add machines that can serve reads and survive node loss, but every write still funnels through the single leader (or still requires coordination in multi-leader/leaderless designs); a write-bound workload needs sharding to split write load across machines, not more copies of the same data
Read replicas can accept writes directly once a quorum of them agrees, but the coordination overhead this requires cancels out any throughput gain
Replicas only copy schema definitions, not row data, so they provide no benefit to any workload, read-heavy or write-heavy
A database with read replicas automatically begins hash-partitioning new writes across those replicas without any additional configuration
explanation: Replication solves the read-capacity and availability ceilings by adding more machines holding copies of the same data, but it does nothing to change how many machines process writes, since writes are still serialized through the leader (or coordinated across leaders/replicas). A genuine write-throughput or storage ceiling requires sharding, which splits the data itself across machines, not additional read replicas.

promptText: Why is single-leader replication, configured to block a write until a majority of followers acknowledge it, described as a CP-leaning design under CAP?
options: It refuses to let two leaders exist and will sacrifice write availability during a leader failure or election rather than risk two authoritative, potentially divergent answers
It always returns the fastest possible read from any node, prioritizing availability over consistency by design
It guarantees sub-millisecond write latency because exactly one node is ever involved in processing a write
It is leaderless by definition, so no single node's failure can ever block a write from succeeding
explanation: Single-leader replication with majority acknowledgment stops accepting writes during a leader failure or election rather than allow a second leader to emerge and risk conflicting authoritative answers, which is exactly the availability-for-consistency trade CP describes. It is not leaderless, and the failover process itself is a real, if brief, write-availability cost.

promptText: Why do most production MySQL and PostgreSQL deployments use semi-synchronous replication rather than waiting for every follower to acknowledge a write?
options: Waiting for every follower couples the leader's write availability to the single slowest or least-reachable follower; semi-synchronous replication bounds durability to at least one follower while avoiding that all-or-nothing fragility
Semi-synchronous replication eliminates replication lag entirely across every follower in the cluster
Fully synchronous replication to every follower is not technically supported by any mainstream relational database engine
Semi-synchronous replication requires the client to manually retry a write if any follower happens to be behind
explanation: Waiting for acknowledgment from every follower means one slow or unreachable follower can stall or block all writes, the same W=N fragility quorum systems face. Semi-synchronous replication waits for just one nearby follower, bounding worst-case data loss without tying write availability to the health of every follower.

promptText: A user updates their profile through the leader, then immediately re-reads it and sees the old value. The database is single-leader with asynchronous replication, and no caching layer is involved. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?
options: Replication lag caused the read to land on a follower that hasn't applied the write yet, violating read-your-writes; the fix is routing that specific read back to the leader or to a follower confirmed to have caught up
A CDN cached the stale profile page, so the fix is purging the CDN's cache for that page
A unique constraint silently rejected the update, so the write never actually took effect on the leader
The write was never acknowledged to the client, so it has not yet been applied anywhere, including the leader
explanation: With asynchronous single-leader replication, there is always some non-zero delay before a follower applies the leader's latest write, so a read routed to a lagging follower immediately after a write can miss it. The standard mitigation is routing read-after-write requests to the leader, or to a follower known to have caught up, rather than making replication fully synchronous.

promptText: A system shards by auto-incrementing user ID using range-based sharding. Six months later, one shard absorbs nearly all new write traffic while the others sit idle. Why does this happen?
options: New records always have the newest, highest ID, so they always fall into the range currently owned by the shard holding the "tail" of the key space, concentrating all new writes there regardless of total shard count
Range-based sharding requires a directory lookup on every write, and that lookup service became the bottleneck
The hash function used internally by range-based sharding is not uniform for sequential inputs
Range-based sharding only ever uses a single shard until that shard reaches its storage capacity limit
explanation: Because keys are assigned to shards by contiguous ranges and new IDs are always the highest issued so far, every newly created record lands on whichever shard currently owns the top of the range, creating a structural hot-shard problem independent of how many shards exist. This is a well-known weakness of range-based sharding with monotonically increasing keys, not a sign of a misconfigured shard count.

promptText: A team switches from range-based to hash-based sharding specifically to eliminate a hot shard. Afterward, a dashboard query for "orders from the last 24 hours" that used to hit one shard starts timing out under load. What changed?
options: Hashing deliberately destroys key ordering, so records that used to be adjacent (recent orders, clustered by time) are now scattered across every shard, turning a query that targeted one contiguous range into an expensive scatter-gather across all shards
Hash-based sharding rebuilds every index from scratch on each write, which slows down all subsequent reads
Hash-based sharding removes support for filtering by date ranges in SQL entirely
Hash-based sharding routes all range-style queries through the directory service instead of directly to shards
explanation: Hash-based sharding distributes keys uniformly by destroying their natural ordering, which is exactly what fixes a sequential-key hot shard, but it means a query that relies on locality (recent orders clustered together) now has to fan out to every shard and merge results instead of hitting one contiguous range. This scatter-gather cost is the direct trade-off for hash-based sharding's even write distribution.

promptText: Why can multi-leader replication produce a write conflict on the same record that single-leader replication structurally cannot?
options: Two independent leaders can each accept a write to the same record before either has received the other's write via cross-replication, making both writes genuinely concurrent with no natural "first"; single-leader replication serializes every write through one authority, so this situation never arises
Multi-leader replication always uses synchronous replication internally, while single-leader replication always uses asynchronous replication
Conflicts only occur in multi-leader setups because they do not maintain a write-ahead log the way single-leader systems do
Single-leader systems have the identical conflict problem, but they hide it from the application using vector clocks
explanation: In single-leader replication there is exactly one node authorized to accept writes, so there is always a single true order of operations and no two writes can be concurrent from the system's point of view. Multi-leader replication allows more than one node to accept writes independently, so two leaders can each accept a conflicting write before either has seen the other's, producing a genuine conflict that single-leader replication cannot create by design.

promptText: In a leaderless, quorum-based cluster, one replica goes offline for ten minutes of routine maintenance, yet writes keep succeeding the whole time with no visible impact. What mechanism makes this possible, and what does it do with the writes meant for the down replica?
options: Sloppy quorum with hinted handoff: a different, reachable replica temporarily accepts and stores the write on the down replica's behalf, holding a hint to forward it once the original replica recovers, letting the write quorum still be satisfied
The coordinator permanently reduces the replication factor N to exclude the down replica going forward
The cluster multicasts every write instantly to the down replica the moment it reconnects, bypassing the need for any handoff
The leader buffers all writes destined for the down replica in its own memory and discards them if the replica does not return within a fixed window
explanation: When a write's target replica is unreachable, sloppy quorum lets a different, reachable node accept the write on its behalf and hold it as a hint to forward once the original node comes back online. This keeps the cluster satisfying the required write quorum without waiting for the down node, preserving write availability through the entire maintenance window.

promptText: A cluster using naive hash(key) mod N sharding scales from N=6 to N'=8 shards. Roughly what fraction of all keys must move, and why does this matter operationally?
options: About 25% of keys (1 − 6/8), a disruptive fraction for adding just two shards; this is exactly why consistent hashing, which bounds the moved fraction to roughly 1/N, is preferred over naive modulus-based sharding
0% of keys, because hash-mod sharding never requires moving existing data when the shard count increases
100% of keys, because any change to N invalidates every key's assignment under modulus-based hashing
Exactly 2 out of every 6 keys, since only the two newly added shards need any data moved onto them
explanation: Using fraction ≈ 1 − min(N, N′)/max(N, N′), going from N=6 to N′=8 gives 1 − 6/8 = 0.25, meaning roughly a quarter of all keys must be relocated even though only new capacity was added. This large, disruptive reshuffling for a modest capacity increase is precisely the operational pain consistent hashing is designed to avoid.

promptText: Why does directory-based sharding introduce a dependency that range-based and hash-based sharding avoid?
options: A client can compute range- or hash-based ownership locally from the key alone with no network call, but directory-based sharding requires consulting an external lookup table on or near every request, making that directory's availability and latency a dependency for every single request
Directory-based sharding cannot support simple point lookups, only full range scans across all shards
Range-based and hash-based sharding also rely on an internal directory service, so there is no meaningful difference in dependency structure
Directory-based sharding eliminates the need for any shard map, since ownership is encoded directly in the key
explanation: Range-based and hash-based sharding let any client determine a key's owning shard purely by computation, with no network round trip required. Directory-based sharding instead requires looking up ownership in an external table on every request, which buys maximum placement flexibility at the cost of making that directory service's availability and latency a critical dependency for the whole system.

promptText: Why is log-shipping (WAL or binlog) replication considered more reliable than statement-based replication?
options: Some SQL statements are non-deterministic (NOW(), auto-increment ordering under concurrency) and can produce different results if independently re-executed on each follower; log-shipping instead replays the leader's exact, already-applied low-level changes, guaranteeing every follower reaches the identical state
Statement-based replication is not supported by any modern relational database engine still in use
Log-shipping replication avoids the need for any network connection between the leader and its followers
Statement-based replication is slower purely because it requires synchronous acknowledgment from every follower before committing
explanation: Re-running SQL statements independently on each follower can diverge when a statement is non-deterministic, since functions like NOW() or concurrency-dependent behaviors can evaluate differently each time. Streaming and replaying the leader's write-ahead log instead guarantees every follower reaches the exact same resulting state, since it replays already-applied changes rather than re-deriving them.

promptText: A team runs the dual-write phase of a live resharding migration but skips the verification/reconciliation phase before cutover. What is the specific risk this creates?
options: A bug in the dual-write logic, such as a silently dropped write or a race with the concurrent backfill, can leave the new shard missing or stale data for some keys; without verification this goes undetected until after cutover, when the old shard's safety net is no longer kept current, turning a recoverable issue into silent, permanent data loss
Skipping verification only adds extra latency to the cutover phase, with no effect on data correctness
Verification only matters for hash-based sharding, so it is safe to omit for a range-based resharding migration
Without verification, the backfill phase simply takes twice as long but still produces an identical, correct result
explanation: Verification exists specifically to catch bugs in dual-write or backfill logic by comparing the old and new shard's contents before anything depends on the new shard being authoritative. Skipping it means such a bug surfaces only after cutover, once the old shard is no longer being kept current as a rollback safety net, converting a detectable, recoverable issue into permanent, silent data loss.

promptText: A multi-tenant SaaS product has a handful of enterprise customers generating roughly 100x the data and traffic of a typical tenant. Why does pure hash-based sharding on tenant ID still produce a hot shard here, and what is the better design?
options: A uniform hash distributes tenants evenly across shards, not the traffic each tenant generates, so one oversized tenant's load still concentrates entirely on whichever shard its hash lands on; the better design hash-shards most tenants normally but explicitly assigns any tenant exceeding a size/traffic threshold its own dedicated shard via a directory
Hash-based sharding guarantees uniform traffic distribution regardless of tenant size, so the hot-shard symptom described must actually be caused by replication lag instead
The correct fix is switching every tenant to range-based sharding keyed on signup date, which naturally isolates large tenants
The correct fix is increasing the number of hash buckets until no single enterprise tenant's share of traffic is statistically significant
explanation: A hash function distributes tenant identifiers evenly, but it says nothing about how much traffic each tenant generates, so a handful of outsized tenants can each concentrate their disproportionate load entirely on whichever single shard they happen to hash to. Combining hash-based sharding for the typical tenant population with a directory-based exception that gives any tenant crossing a size or traffic threshold its own dedicated shard isolates that load without abandoning the simpler scheme for everyone else.

promptText: You are designing the data tier for an inventory system where overselling the last unit of a product is unacceptable. How should replication and sharding be designed, referencing the CP/AP trade-off?
options: Treat inventory as CP-leaning: use single-leader replication with synchronous or semi-synchronous acknowledgment and route decrements through the leader, and shard by product or SKU ID so the "don't oversell this SKU" invariant only ever needs coordination within a single shard, never across shards
Use multi-leader replication across regions so stock decrements can be applied locally everywhere, resolving any conflicting concurrent decrements with last-writer-wins
Use leaderless replication with a write quorum of W=1 to maximize availability for checkout, since availability matters more than consistency for an inventory decrement
Shard inventory by warehouse location so that a single SKU's stock count is deliberately split evenly across multiple shards, reducing per-shard write pressure
explanation: Overselling is a direct correctness failure, making inventory a CP-leaning concern that should favor single-leader replication with synchronous or semi-synchronous acknowledgment to avoid losing an acknowledged decrement on leader failure. Sharding by product or SKU ID keeps the one invariant that matters most confined to a single shard, so the hardest consistency requirement never needs an expensive and often poorly-supported cross-shard transaction.

promptText: A financial ledger needs lower write latency for users in multiple regions. Why is it important to distinguish region-affinity sharding from true multi-leader replication when proposing a solution, rather than treating them as the same idea?
options: Region-affinity sharding keeps each shard single-leader with that leader placed in a given region, so a region's writes are genuinely local with zero conflict risk; true multi-leader replication lets the same shard accept writes from multiple leaders, introducing the conflict-resolution burden that is unacceptable for a ledger needing one unambiguous transaction order
The two approaches are functionally identical, differing only in the terminology different database vendors use for the same mechanism
Region-affinity sharding actually requires more conflict-resolution logic than multi-leader replication, since each shard has a different leader to reconcile against
True multi-leader replication is strictly safer for a ledger, since every write is acknowledged by multiple leaders before being confirmed to the client
explanation: Region-affinity sharding still gives each shard exactly one leader, just placed near the region that owns that shard's data, so local writes have no conflicting counterpart to reconcile against. True multi-leader replication allows the same shard to accept writes from more than one leader, reintroducing the conflict-detection and resolution burden that is specifically unacceptable for a ledger's need for one unambiguous, auditable order of transactions.
